extracted.intended_audience: writers, dramatists, poets, rhetoricians, literary critics, and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating dramatic and poetic works (tragedy, epic, comedy) and for achieving elevated/sublime diction in rhetoric and literature, covering plot, character, diction, thought, melody, spectacle, unity, catharsis, and principles of the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is an imitation of human life; its art is an imitation by movement and is therefore allied with the time-arts (dance, music) rather than the space-arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: treat poetic art as representation of action and life rather than mere chronicling; the imitator selects and arranges actions to convey universals rather than singular events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of imitation: rhythm, language, harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The means of imitation in the arts are rhythm, language, and harmony—used singly or in combination; e.g., flute/lyre use rhythm+melody, dance uses rhythm alone, and certain prose/verse use language alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate means for the genre: tragedy and epic combine language and rhythm; dithyrambic and nomic poetry may combine all three. Meter influences perceived 'speakability' (iambic is most speakable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: actions and agents
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitator represents actions with agents who are either good, bad, or like ourselves; these distinctions determine the kind of poetry (tragedy, epic, comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select agents appropriate to genre: tragedy typically portrays agents 'better than we are', comedy 'worse than average', and other forms vary; moral quality shapes character depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: narrative, assumed character, dramatic acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation may be effected by narrative alternated with assumed character (Homer), by remaining the same (authorial voice), or by representing the story dramatically as if actors were doing the things described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work will be primarily narrative, dialogic/character-driven, or performative, as this affects unity, immediacy, and mode of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is the imitation of an action that is serious and also, as having magnitude, complete in itself; in language with pleasurable accessories; in a dramatic, not a narrative form; with incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure seriousness, unity of action, suitable language (with rhythm/melody where appropriate), dramatic presentation, and emotionally effective incidents that lead to catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The six constituent parts of tragedy are: plot (fable), character, diction, thought, spectacle, and melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to evaluate or compose tragedy; recognize that some parts arise from means (diction, melody), some from manner (spectacle), and some from objects (plot, character, thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot (fable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important of the six parts is the combination of the incidents of the story (the plot); tragedy is essentially an imitation of action and life, and the plot is the life and soul of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize constructing a coherent, necessary/probable sequence of incidents; a strong plot can outweigh superior diction or character work in producing tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole (plot) must have a beginning, middle, and end: a beginning is not necessarily after anything, the middle follows and precedes, and the end follows but has nothing after it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so that removal of any one incident dislocates the whole; aim for an organic unity rather than simply focusing on one protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot represents one complete action (probable or necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet describes a kind of thing that might happen—what is possible as being probable or necessary—rather than merely recounting what did happen; poetry states universals while history states singulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose incidents that cohere as a single action with causal or probable connections; even when using known names, retain probability and universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripety and discovery as devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A peripety is a reversal from one state to its opposite in the probable/necessary sequence; a discovery is a change from ignorance to knowledge. The finest discoveries are those attended by peripeties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals and revelations that arise inevitably from antecedent events to arouse pity and fear and to bring about the ending; avoid contrived surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are simple when change in fortunes occurs without peripety or discovery; complex when it involves one or both (peripety/discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with well-integrated reversals/discoveries) generally have finer tragic effect; design plot structure to produce emotional impact through these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic plot as an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic plot lacks probability or necessity in the sequence of its episodes; such plots are the worst and result from either the poet's fault or pressure from players/theatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stringing loosely-connected episodes; ensure causal/probable links between scenes so the plot holds as a single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by motivation and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A character is convincing—real and significant—by motivation and by working out his dramatic destiny; character gives us moral purpose and reveals what agents seek or avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters' actions stem from consistent motivations; prioritize motivation-driven behavior over mere descriptive traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) distinct from character
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the power of saying whatever can be said or what is appropriate to the occasion; it shows in speeches when proving a point or enunciating general truth, and is different from character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop arguments and lines of reasoning appropriate to characters and situations; in speeches, thought is the domain of political/rhetorical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) and style
rubrics_metrics.description: By diction is meant the composition of the verses—the expression of thoughts in words; diction and style are among the formative elements of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words, meters, and phrasing appropriate to character and genre; diction affects tone and the pleasurable quality of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody and spectacle roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (song) is the greatest of the pleasurable accessories of tragedy; spectacle (the visual appearance) is the least artistic part and has least to do with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate musical/rhythmic elements in language where fitting; do not rely on spectacle to produce the essential tragic effect—plot and language are primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy vs epic: unity and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from tragedy in being narrative, in length, and in scope; tragedy is superior in intensity through unity, while epic gives pleasure of ranging and variety but is less intense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For concentrated emotional effect aim for tragedy's unity; for breadth and variety employ epic modes but accept lower intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of comedy (the ridiculous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of men worse than the average in the particular kind of fault called the ridiculous—defined as a mistake or deformity not productive of pain or harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comic composition emphasize the ludicrous without cruelty; the ridiculous should not cause true harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet vs historian: universals over singulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet states universals (what such a kind of man will probably or necessarily say or do) while the historian records singular events (what Alcibiades did).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, generalize from particulars to reveal universal human truths rather than merely recording facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude/length of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot must be of a magnitude to be taken in by the memory; roughly, a length that allows the hero to pass by a series of probable or necessary stages from misfortune to happiness, or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the story long enough for development but short enough to be apprehended as a whole; adjust length to comprehensibility and dramatic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solutions and endings must arise from the plot (no stage artifice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic solution should 'arise out of the plot itself,' result inevitably from the course of action, not be foisted on the play by interference from outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deus ex machina or contrived endings; make every climactic event flow from antecedent motives and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity: greatness of thought / nobility of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime (height) arises from greatness of thought—noble ideas and loftiness of conception which lift utterance above the commonplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate grand and elevated conceptions; the author's moral and imaginative grasp (greatness of soul) is a primary source of sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity: passionate ardor / strong emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong emotion or 'fervour of soul' (ardor) is a source of the sublime; passion energizes diction and produces lofty utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let genuine passion infuse language—forced or simulated emotion will not produce true sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity: noble and appropriate diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime depends on suitable, lofty word-choice and diction; lofty passages must avoid descending to sordid or petty language unless overwhelmingly necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain register appropriate to subject matter; do not mix trivial items or coarse vocabulary into elevated passages as this produces deformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagery, metaphor, and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery and figures are the verbal means of giving effect to intellectual conception and emotional suggestion; metaphor and figures should be used so well they are 'not noticed as a figure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ fresh, apt metaphors and images that reveal rather than merely decorate; avoid strained or ostentatious figures that call attention to themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence rhythm and harmonious arrangement (periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence rhythm (harmonious arrangement) and carefully rounded periods are fundamental to elevated style; rhythm in sentence structure enhances mood and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the musicality of sentences and to balanced, rhythmic periods especially in oratory and high prose; vary cadence to suit emotional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial enumeration and low-detail in lofty description
rubrics_metrics.description: In lofty passages one ought not to descend to sordid and contemptible language; e.g., enumerating bags, condiments, and sacks in a magnificent description creates offensiveness and triviality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing grandeur, rise higher in generalizing or choose elevated particulars; avoid petty or shopkeeper-like details that degrade tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate ascent and amplification in description
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions should rise and climb to higher things (ascent) rather than descend from noble to paltry; amplification must be ordered to heighten effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure descriptive sequences to increase magnitude and emotional elevation; descending order or irrelevant detail dissipates grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral earnestness and purpose (authorial temperament)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is allied to moral earnestness and the artist's missionary zeal; great authors satisfy the longing to enter the human scene fully and to touch heights of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate seriousness of aim and moral/intellectual depth; sublimity is rooted in the author's temperament and aims, not mere stylistic tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing registers and irrelevant minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing low and high elements (e.g., gold goblets and petty sacks in one register) offends and creates deformity in style; trivial opposites spoil noble diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent register; where contrast is needed, ensure it is motivated and artistically justified rather than jarring or gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeches must suit the speaker's social/mental role
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons should discourse appropriately to their role: older poets have personages speak like statesmen, modern ones like rhetoricians; thought and diction must fit character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match rhetorical level, argumentation, and diction to the character's station, education, and temperament to preserve verisimilitude.
